tagline: A 3D periodic table to walk into, for Artur and his father.

waiting.title: Play today's element with Artur
waiting.detail: On the plaza, tap the 🔥 at the bottom left and play the day's lesson (about three minutes), each on your own account. Tomorrow open it again: the mystery is revealed and the streak grows. Tell me here what Artur makes of the streak and the questions.

waiting.title: Listen on your phone: is the crackle gone?
waiting.detail: Open the game on the phone (tap Reload if it offers a new version), walk through the plaza, a hall and a lab with the sound on, and tick this. If you still hear crackling, send a note saying where. The game now counts its own crackles, so the next session can check your phone's count too.

waiting.title: Try the two made-over halls with Artur: sodium and silicon
waiting.detail: Each has its picture boards, a showpiece, a doorway board you step into, and a Periodic Videos lab with the film beside the experiments, the professor's own lines, and the view through the Atomling's eyes at each station. Note what to keep and what to change before the next ones.

waiting.title: Play the newest things with Artur
waiting.detail: The breathing exhibit in the air wing, the neon sign workshop, the Atom Forge, a room played together, and how the Atomlings look. One line in a note is enough: what he liked, what bored him.

waiting.title: Let Claude measure the game on your phone
waiting.detail: Once, on the Galaxy S21: Settings, Developer options, Wireless debugging on, with the phone on the same Wi-Fi as the computer. Tick this, and the next session measures every world on the phone itself (so far only the hall and the graphene gallery).

waiting.title: Rate krypton's rooms and the cost trial
waiting.detail: Krypton's seven rooms were built by Sonnet 5.5 at high effort, radon's will be built by Opus 5.5 at xhigh. Open the hall, step into a few rooms, and give the card under Built its stars: 3 or more means you would keep it as it is. The table in What it cost then shows which setting earned its price.

items.title: Doing things together in the worlds
items.summary: In a room, the things in a world are shared: you let the balloons go in the neon workshop and everyone there sees them rise; whoever comes in later finds them up under the ceiling. Panels, the Atomling's words and videos stay each one's own.
details: Done (2026-10-30): every wing. The neon workshop (the tubes, the radon counter, the word on the wall, the atom, the history board, the spectroscope, the balloons), carbon's gallery (14 exhibits) and garden (9), oxygen's air deck (7) and fire chamber (5), sodium's lab (4) and silicon's (5). The halls share nothing: what you do there is reading, going through a door or talking.

Each world is saved twice, as you asked: your own (on the device and in your account) and each room's. The room keeps its worlds even when nobody is in them: come back to the room later and the balloons are still up, the word still on the wall. A room's world starts fresh, never from anyone's own; leave the room and your own is back.

Discoveries and badges count the same alone or in a room, and only for the one who does it. Standing beside someone who just tried something you have not, you get a note: try it yourself to make it your discovery.
The video, its parts and every panel stay each one's own, as you asked; so do the Atomling's and the professor's words.
How it works: one mechanism for every world, and each exhibit says what its state is and how to replay it (a new wing does the same; a probe flags any exhibit that shares nothing).

items.title: Picture boards for every hall
items.summary: The fact file, seven picture boards and a showpiece that Carbon and Oxygen have, for the other 116 halls.
items.why: Every visit passes through a hall, so this changes the most. Element by element, each new picture with its room (your rule); the Periodic Videos rooms wait (Later). The 38 elements Artur meets first (the quiz's Explorer list) before the rest.
details: Done (2026-10-30): sodium (nerves, the sea and Aveiro's salt pans, Davy 1807, the yellow street lamps, sodium 90 km up, the cake that rises) and silicon (diatoms' glass houses, solar cells, sand into glass, the rocky Earth and Moon, Silicon Valley, silicone bakeware), each with its doorway board and a showpiece. Next by the dashboard's visits, then the rest of the quiz's well-known elements.
Carbon and Oxygen got them first because the eight text boards were boring. You loved them (2026-10-29), so the others follow.
Each board is a picture with a hook question, read in Explorer or Scientist; the fact file has a face drawn from the element's data; the showpiece is a real-looking sample in the museum case.

In batches of five or six: first the 38 well-known elements of the quiz's Explorer list (hydrogen to plutonium), then the rest family by family. Each batch is checked in all four languages and looked at in the game before it goes live, and goes live as soon as it is done.
Each element's Periodic Videos video and its own story in the game are the research notes; every number comes from the game's data.
The well-known elements get a showpiece of their own, as Carbon and Oxygen did; the rest keep the museum case's samples.

Hydrogen done (2026-10-31): seven pictures, each a room: the young universe cooling into the first atoms, Charles's balloon over the Tuileries in 1783, a pond at a skater's size, a hydrogen filling station by a railway, Cavendish's laboratory where fire makes water, a gondola sinking into Jupiter, the Dwingeloo dish listening for the 21 cm line; its showpiece a spectrum tube glowing pink-violet beside a balloon. Each hall in two steps: the boards and room designs, then the rooms (docs/agents/).

Iron done (2026-10-31): the Hoba meteorite and Tutankhamun's dagger, a research ship over the Earth's iron dynamo, an Iron Age smith, iron pulled from breakfast cereal, the Eiffel Tower's rivets and its top leaning from the sun, Opportunity on Mars, a thermite weld on a railway; its showpiece an etched iron meteorite. Next: krypton's and radon's seven rooms each: their pictures are drawn and their rooms designed (docs/agents/designs/), waiting to go up together with the rooms.

Model trial (2026-10-31): krypton's rooms built with Sonnet 5.5 at high effort, radon's with Opus 5.5 at xhigh, so "What it cost" can compare the two on the same kind of work; your stars on both decide which builds the rooms after that.

Krypton done (2026-11-01, the model trial's first half: rooms built on Sonnet 5.5 at high effort): seven pictures, each a room: the last drops of liquid air in 1898, the metre from the 1889 bar to light itself, the window factory, a platform in orbit with a Hall thruster, an oasis and the atom trap that dates a million-year-old water, krypton holding hands with fluorine, and the night gallery where kryptonite meets jadarite; its showpiece a lilac glowing globe and krypton frozen white. Next: radon's seven rooms on Opus 5.5 at xhigh, the trial's other half (docs/agents/designs/Rn_rooms.md).

items.title: Periodic Videos rooms
items.summary: Each element gets a room where the experiments from its Periodic Videos video (Brady Haran with Professor Sir Martyn Poliakoff, University of Nottingham) are rebuilt as things you do, with the video beside them: watch to understand, do it yourself, go back to the video for the why.
items.why: You marked it Later (2026-10-30): sodium's and silicon's rooms stay as they are, and no new video rooms until the forges and the halls have had their turn.
details: Two rooms are built (2026-10-30): sodium's and silicon's (the glittering lump and sand, the chip line, the wafer's rainbow, the turbocharger race, the minerals).

Sodium's room is built (2026-10-30), the pilot to try: the oil tin, the courtyard bowl with three lumps and the indicator, the salt window, the salt lamp, the professor's card, and the film on the screen with a chapter per experiment.

The lab is entered through a doorway board in the hall (step into the picture); the professor stands in it and retells his own remarks from the film, each with the moment to watch him say it. Using a station in third person now looks through the Atomling's eyes.

Claude watches each video (a frame every 4 seconds with the captions, in a cache on this computer that never goes online) and writes a brief: what the video shows, with times, and the room's stations.

Sodium's video, watched 2026-10-30: cutting a two-kilo rod from its oil tin (soft, shiny, white within seconds), a gram in a bowl of water in a courtyard (skating, fizzing, the orange flame), a salt window that cracks at right angles, a rock-salt lamp, and a bigger lump with a bang. All five become stations (docs/pv/Na.md).
Each station has 'Watch this part': the video plays from that experiment's moment, in YouTube's own player, credited and linked to periodicvideos.com.
The game retells everything in its own words with its own numbers; the video's footage and words stay the video's. Dangerous experiments keep the video's warning: never at home.

One shared room dressed per element (a lab bench, a fume cupboard, a door to a brick courtyard, the professor's desk), and a kit used again and again: the water bowl for every alkali metal, flame colours, fizz, smoke, liquid nitrogen, a Geiger counter. Apparatus modelled in Blender where it looks better than code.
The door to it: a doorway board in each hall lists the element's extra places (its wings, this room, the hunts that start there) and makes room as more arrive, your blackboard idea.

items.title: Step into the pictures
items.summary: Artur's first question when he saw the new boards: how do I get inside these pictures? Every picture board becomes a doorway, like the Periodic Videos one: you dive into the picture and stand inside its scene, a small place made from the picture itself, with one to three things to do and the board's story told there.
details: A ladder of three steps. A picture room for every board, in time: a small scene around where you land, built from a shared kit of stages (a place indoors or outdoors, the sky and space, the very small, a moment in history) and parts, mostly written as data, with one to three things to do. A room that turns out loved (the family dashboard shows the visits) or whose subject keeps growing becomes a full wing like carbon's, at the same address, so nothing breaks. The big wings (carbon, oxygen, the neon signs) keep their arches.

Your rule (2026-10-30): no picture without its room. The pictures already on the walls (silicon, sodium, carbon, oxygen) get their rooms, silicon first; every new hall from now on is drawn and built picture and room together.

Silicon is done (2026-10-30): all six of its pictures are doors. The diatoms (a sunlit sea floor), solar (a hilltop: the sun on a slider, light fired into a giant cell, Vanguard 1), glass (a glassblower's workshop: fill the pot, blow a bottle, light through sand, glass and fibre), the Earth and Moon (a deck in space: the Earth cut open, Moon rocks, a star that makes silicon), Silicon Valley (a hilltop at night: the valley from 1950 to today, a giant transistor, the 4004's 2300 lights) and silicone (a kitchen: the bendy tray, the snapping silicon, the putty, the chain). Next: sodium's six pictures, then carbon's and oxygen's.

Sodium is done (2026-10-30): beside a giant nerve fibre (fire the nerve, the sodium pump, the race), Aveiro's salt pans (the sea salted by rain and volcanoes, the ponds, the marnoto's rake), Davy's lab of 1807 (the battery, the soda split into beads of sodium, his desk), a street at night (the lamp warming from pink to yellow, colours that vanish, the spectroscope), a mountaintop observatory (the laser guide star, the twinkle taken out, shooting stars and Hale-Bopp) and a baking kitchen (the fizz test, two cakes, soda heated alone). Then carbon's.

Carbon is done (2026-10-30): the diamond depths and the pencil workshop (twins), inside a body (the recipe in jars, the DNA zipper, bread into you), inside a leaf (van Helmont's willow, the stoma, RuBisCO), beside a red giant (the triple-alpha catch, Hoyle's ladder, carbon into space), an archaeologists' dig (carbon-14 made in the sky, dating the finds, the hourglass of atoms), Smalley's lab of 1985 (the peak at 60, the paper ball, nanotubes stronger than steel) and Mauna Loa (the coal forest, the Keeling curve, the heat blanket).

Oxygen is done (2026-10-31): a ride on a red blood cell from the lung to a working muscle (breath), Lavoisier's laboratory with Priestley's burning lens and the twelve days (fire, at /e/O/fire-picture since the fire wing has /e/O/fire), an Antarctic station where the ozone hole was found and fixed (ozone), a shore 2.5 billion years ago with its rusting sea (first), a bathhouse by a frozen lake with the bath on a balance (water), a camp in Lapland under the aurora (aurora), a cold lab with liquid air, the floating frog and a rocket (magnet). Every picture on a wall is now a door; new halls bring their pictures and rooms together (halls-116).
No size limit in the code: a room can be any size or shape. The kit is there so that about seven hundred of them can be made at all, open quickly and run well on the phone.

Size is not what slows things down: each world's code is fetched only when you go in (carbon's gallery 310 KB, a hall 45 KB) and freed when you leave. What costs is the first visit's shader compiling (1.2 to 3.9 s now; carbon's gallery needs 53 programs; rooms made from one kit share theirs, so the second room opens almost at once) and, on the phone, how much is drawn at once (lights, glass, particles).

The board's story (four languages, both depths) is told inside, so a room adds only the words for its own things to do. Some existing ideas are rooms that grew: Aveiro's salt pans is sodium's salt board; Walk inside a chip could grow out of silicon's Silicon Valley board.

items.title: Treasure hunts
items.summary: Hunts in order: each clue leads to the next hall, board or exhibit, on a theme.
items.why: Hunts turn everything already built into a game to play again, alone or as a team. They are best once the halls have their boards, so they come right after.
details: Themes: history (who found what, and when), uses (where you meet the element at home), records (the heaviest, the coldest, the rarest), general knowledge, and more as the world grows.
Difficulty from Explorer clues to Scientist riddles. A long hunt can be left and picked up later: your progress stays in your account, a team's under its room code.

Built from what is in the game, so every answer can be found there. Each clue points at a real place, and the tests fail when a place a hunt needs goes away, so hunts stay true without an update schedule. New tracks come after a batch of new content, and a hunt in progress keeps the version it started with.
A few tracks first; many more once the usage data shows that hunts are played often.

items.title: Scavenger hunts
items.summary: A list of things to find in any order: every noble gas's sign, three elements found in the 1700s, the metal that is liquid.
items.why: Quick to play together, and it builds on the rooms and the duel that are already there.
details: Together: a room shares one list and everyone's finds count.
Race: the same list for everyone, first to find all wins; the quiz duel's seats and watchers carry over.
A home edition later: find elements around the house (salt, kitchen foil, a pencil's graphite) and tick them off.

items.title: The star forge
items.summary: Make the elements as the universe did: fuse hydrogen into helium inside a star and climb toward iron; heavier elements need neutrons, caught slowly in old giant stars or all at once when neutron stars collide.
details: Explorer: pick a star's size and watch which elements it can make before it dies. Scientist: the burning stages, their temperatures and how long each lasts, the slow and rapid neutron captures.
Every element made lights up on the table, with where the atoms in your body came from.

Built (2026-10-31) at /stars: a nursery of stars (a red dwarf to 25 suns, or a mass slider); tap the core through its burnings in a cutaway; its end (a white dwarf, a supernova, a pulsar or a black hole); the slow catch inside an old giant from iron to lead and the rapid catch in two merging neutron stars to gold and uranium; the table lit by where each element came from, and where your own atoms came from. Twelve missions in the passport. Next ideas: an exploding white dwarf (iron and manganese), the rapid catch weighted into a real abundance curve, a check on your phone.

items.title: The forge together
items.summary: The Atom Forge in a room: build one nucleus together, or race each other to a mission.
details: The next step for rooms (docs/knowledge/multiplayer.md).

Built (2026-10-31): in a room everyone builds one atom (every press counts, the others' particles fly in glowing in their colour, a line says who did what, missions done together count for everyone there); anyone can start a race to a mission (a countdown, each builds their own atom, a board shows how far each is, the first wins, then back to the shared atom). Ideas next: a head start for the younger racer, best of three, watching one racer's atom.

items.title: Ride with a red blood cell
items.summary: Follow the oxygen you just breathed: into the lungs, onto haemoglobin, through the heart to a working muscle.
details: Oxygen's third world, starting from the breathing exhibit in the air wing.

Built as oxygen's breath picture room (2026-10-31): breathe in, look inside a red cell at its haemoglobin, ride it through the heart to a muscle, the muscle's power stations. It can grow into a full wing if it turns out loved.

items.title: Collect your Atomlings
items.summary: Finishing a hall's exhibits wins its Atomling for your team; your team follows you around, and a whole family earns its badge.
details: A reason to visit every hall, kept in the account. The characters stay the game's own.

items.title: Today's element and the streak
items.summary: One element a day, the same for the whole family: a three-minute lesson, a streak with freezes for a day missed, and tomorrow's element as a mystery to guess.
details: Built (2026-11-09), after the brainstorm on what brings a player back between sessions; you: "Artur already is hooked on duolingo's streaks so might work fine".
The lesson: find the day's element in the table (its Atomling pops up and says hello), three questions about it, two elements met before, the missed ones once more; every answer says why.
The streak forgives: one freeze to start, one more every seventh day (two at most). Elements answered right come back after 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 days; sleepy Atomlings wait for the ones due.
Tomorrow's mystery: two clues and four to choose from, the same for everyone, so you and Artur can argue about it before it comes.
The flame is the first button in the plaza's dock; the passport has the streak and two badges (7 and 30 days). The days follow the account to any device.

items.title: Molecule race
items.summary: In a room, the same molecule for everyone: first to build it wins, then a harder one.
details: The competitive side of the shared Molecule Lab.

items.title: The magnet and motor workshop
items.summary: Build an electric motor; compare iron, ferrite and neodymium magnets lifting weights; why wind turbines and electric cars need rare earths.
details: One wing shared by iron, cobalt, nickel, neodymium, samarium and dysprosium, like the neon sign workshop.

items.title: The particle accelerator
items.summary: Fire a calcium beam at a target and, maybe once a week, make one atom of a new element that lasts a thousandth of a second; the island of stability.
details: Shared by the superheavy elements, 104 to 118. The Atom Forge's beam already does the reactions.

items.title: Inside the Sun
items.summary: In the Sun's core four hydrogens become helium and light comes out; a hydrogen car whose exhaust is water; the lightest gas lifting a balloon.

items.title: Superfluid helium
items.summary: Helium cooled near absolute zero creeps up the walls of its cup and out.
details: The 1868 eclipse, where helium was found in sunlight, is already on the neon workshop's spectroscope.

items.title: The battery factory
items.summary: Lithium-ion cells charging a scooter; the lightest metal floating on oil.

items.title: The liquid nitrogen lab
items.summary: At minus 196 °C a flower shatters and ice cream sets at once; the nitrogen cycle in the soil, with the bacteria on bean roots.

items.title: Aveiro's salt pans (sodium and chlorine)
items.summary: Table salt crystals growing in the salt pans; why sodium must never touch water, watched behind glass.
details: Built as sodium's picture room behind the hall's picture "Why is the sea salty?" (2026-10-30): the model of rain, rivers and a volcano salting the sea, three ponds you work by their gates with a sun-and-wind slider, flor de sal, the marnoto's rake.

items.title: Fireworks and chlorophyll
items.summary: Magnesium's white fire, and the magnesium at the green heart of every leaf.

items.title: From bauxite to a can and back
items.summary: Recycling a can saves about 95% of the energy of making it new.

items.title: Walk inside a chip
items.summary: From sand to a chip, then inside a processor where the transistors are buildings.
details: Your note (2026-10-30): build it from the video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vuvckBQ1bME in two versions of the journey: one following the video's amusing steps as its author did, one from Claude's own research and design. Then compare which the family likes (an A/B test), or keep both and let the player choose (two interiors of the room, or both paths in one big room). The video is fast: look at it at more than one frame a second (tools/pv/pv.py zoom at 4 or more frames a second, not only the 2 s sheets).

items.title: The match factory
items.summary: Matches, the backbone of DNA, and Hennig Brand's glowing flask of 1669.

items.title: The volcano crater
items.summary: Yellow sulfur crystals growing round the vents of a crater.

items.title: The reef and the limestone cave
items.summary: A coral reef, stalactites growing in a cave, and your own skeleton.

items.title: The jet engine
items.summary: Titanium in a jet engine's fan and in a hip implant.

items.title: The blacksmith's forge
items.summary: Heat, hammer and quench to make steel; a journey to the Earth's core; the iron in red blood.

items.title: The electricity hall
items.summary: Wires, a dynamo and lights; the Statue of Liberty turning green.

items.title: The darkroom
items.summary: A photographer's darkroom, and the shiniest mirror.

items.title: The light bulb factory
items.summary: Tungsten, the metal with the highest melting point, glowing in a bulb.

items.title: The treasure vault
items.summary: Gold leaf thinner than a hair is wide, and gold born when neutron stars collide.

items.title: The liquid metal
items.summary: The old thermometer, and a steel ball floating on mercury.

items.title: The reactor's control room
items.summary: A chain-reaction game: catch the neutrons with the control rods.

items.title: Alloys at the forge
items.summary: Metals mixed into bronze, brass and steel (iron with a little carbon).

items.title: Reactions in the lab
items.summary: Burning methane, rusting and photosynthesis as a game, with the atoms counted on both sides.
details: Methane and rust are already benches in oxygen's fire wing, and photosynthesis is carbon's tree; the game in the lab is not built yet.

items.title: Rings and life
items.summary: Benzene, glucose and the four DNA bases; build a short strand of DNA.

items.title: Crystals that grow
items.summary: Ions stacking into a salt crystal you can watch grow.
details: The lab already makes ionic compounds (2026-10-28); the growing crystal is the missing part.

items.title: Faster first visits
items.summary: A world seen for the first time takes 1.2 to 3.9 s to appear; fewer kinds of material would cut that.
details: Carbon's gallery still needs 53 shader programs.

items.title: See through lattices
items.summary: The third-person camera keeps clear of walls, but lattices and treetops can still get in its way; each world needs its own fade.

items.title: Every world measured on the phone
items.summary: Frame times on the Galaxy S21 for every world, not only the hall and the graphene gallery.
details: Waits on Wireless debugging (Waiting on you).

items.title: Every station worked by hand
items.summary: Your rule for every station: you choose each step by clicking or tapping the thing it is about (the sand, the soda, the pot), and anything that changes smoothly is a slider; pressing E again and again felt passive.
details: The picture rooms follow it from now on (the diatoms already: tap the round diatom, the boat diatoms in the sun, the family). The older worlds still step through some stations with E: carbon's and oxygen's wings, the neon workshop and the two video labs could get the same treatment, station by station.

Carbon's two wings are done (2026-10-31): peel graphene by tapping the stack, slide graphite's layers, the transistor's gate as a slider and the chip tapped to swap plain graphene for two layers, the diamond press in five taps (graphite on the tray, the pump lever, the capsule, the piston, the diamond), the garden's sunlight as a slider, the carbon-14 clock and its jar. Every one-step exhibit takes a tap too.

Done (2026-10-31): oxygen's two wings (a molecule or a gas column to count, two flasks at the magnet, land or sea on the globe, the fire triangle's sides, the jar, the splint, sliders for the Great Oxidation and the rust), the neon workshop (any gas in any order, the ladder's lines, the spectroscope's rack, one balloon at a time) and the two video labs (the tin and the knife, lumps by the bowl, the lamp switch, the chip tester and wafer board, the minerals in a row). Every station in the game is worked by hand now.

items.title: Bible passages in every place
items.summary: Your request: passages from the Bible throughout the world, each about the place it stands in; the NLT for Explorer and the CSB for Scientist.
details: Built (2026-10-31): every hall has a verse stone across from its specimen case, with the element's own passage where the Bible has one (iron sharpens iron, gold as clear as glass, the rainbow in iridium's name, sand for silicon), else one for its name (countries, scientists) or its family. The wings have theirs (the burning bush beside the campfire, let your light shine in the neon workshop, the many works of one hand under carbon's motto), the plaza, the lab and both forges write theirs in the sky, and the quiz and the Atomlings page carry one. A tap or E opens it with a line on why it is there.
Every passage’s popup opens it in the Bible App (your idea, 2026-10-31): right on the verse, in the translation the level quotes, where the whole chapter and the app’s pictures for it are.

The other languages quote their own pair: Bíblia para Todos and Almeida Corrigida (Portugal), the EIB's Bible and Biblia Warszawska, Hoffnung für alle and Schlachter 2000. The About box lists the publishers' notices.
Not yet: the picture rooms and the video rooms (an idea below).

items.title: Passages in the picture rooms
items.summary: Every hall and world has its Bible passage now; the rooms inside the pictures and the video rooms could have one each, where the picture's subject has one (the Tyrian purple room, the salt mine, the stars).
details: The pieces are ready (a stone, a wall plaque, words in the sky): a passage is a line in a list, its words fetched by a tool, and a few lines in the room.

items.title: The diamond press for two
items.summary: Your request: stations two people can play and have fun with, like Experimentarium's and the Copernicus Centre's; some alone, some more fun together, some needing another person. One working example.
details: Built (2026-10-31): carbon's diamond press. One pumps at the red lever (the seals leak; too much opens the safety valve), the other works the heater (its screen shows the window where diamond grows). The diamond grows only while both are right, for 45 seconds, then the press opens on it: about a carat with good teamwork.
Alone you do both jobs (hard). In a room, with two or more at the press, whoever takes a job keeps it and the other is told “Ana has that job. Call out to them!”. Someone leaving frees their job.

items.title: More stations for two
items.summary: After the diamond press, the same pattern elsewhere: a job that really takes two (or three) things at once, split between players, alone still possible.
details: The fire triangle for three: each holds one side (fuel, heat, oxygen), the fire burns only while all three hold.
The neon bench: one pumps the vacuum, the other fills the gas and switches on the high voltage.
An electron tug of war between two atoms: who wins is the electronegativity, so the fun is in choosing your atom.

items.title: The moiré turns differently for two players
items.summary: The room check of carbon's gallery finds the moiré turntable's state differing between two players after its button (one turning by hand, the other sweeping). It is on the live site too, older than the press.
details: tools/shared_probe.py --world /e/C/allotropes: five checks, all the moiré's.

items.title: A dark bar in a phone view
items.summary: In the phone's station view of krypton's clean-up (room hidden) a thin dark bar stands in front of the bench; it does not show on a computer and the builder could not trace it.
details: Seen in the builder's shot kr_h_ph2 (Portuguese, upright phone). Hiding everything above 2.9 m or beyond 5.5 m did not remove it, so it may be a stand's leg or part of the Atomling.

items.title: Check clouds of dots on the phone
items.summary: Krypton's first room draws a million additive dots for a jar of air; a computer is fine, the Galaxy S21 was never measured.
details: Measure the frame rate in room hidden on the phone (tools/phone.py); if it drops, draw fewer dots and say 'about a million'.

items.title: The family streak
items.summary: On the daily sheet, who in the family has done today's element; a shared flame on the days you both did, and "your turn" when one is waiting.
details: Artur and his father keeping each other going, the way Duolingo's friend streaks do. Needs a way to say who is family (the accounts are the Pokémon site's, shared with others).

items.title: A reminder at an hour you choose
items.summary: If today's element is still waiting at the hour the family picks, the installed game sends one gentle notification.
details: Half of Duolingo's hold is its reminder. A phone's home-screen app can show notifications (Android, and iPhone since iOS 16.4); it needs permission, a little server that sends them, and a way to switch it off.

items.title: The element hunt at home
items.summary: A list for the week: find something at home with iron, with sodium, with copper... a tick or a photo, and it goes into the passport.
details: Moves the learning into the house between sessions: every spoon and tap becomes a reminder of the game.

items.title: A radon clock
items.summary: Radon gathered in the Atom Forge halves every 3.8 days on the real clock: come back to see how much is left, and gather more.
details: Half-life learned by waiting for it. Fits radon's hall, which comes next.

items.title: A question to take away
items.summary: Each hall ends on one open question whose answer is in another hall or world ("Krypton glows lilac: why would a gas that never reacts glow at all?").
details: A question left open is what makes a player think about it until the next visit.

items.title: Mail from the Atomlings
items.summary: Short notes waiting on the plaza when you come back: "Sodium here: I just exploded in a lake, come and see!"
details: Each note leads somewhere in the game; they come from the elements met and the ones waiting to be gone over.

items.title: Riddles for each other
items.summary: Artur writes a "Who am I?" riddle for his father, and the other way round; the answer waits for the other's next visit.
details: Making clues is the best way to learn the facts, and the game already has the clue format.

items.title: A duel over days
items.summary: The quiz duel played one question a day each, like chess by post.
details: For days when you are not together in a room.

items.title: Predict element 119
items.summary: After the superheavy halls, guess the next element's properties, keep the guess in a time capsule and open it a month later.
details: Science as predicting and checking; the superheavies' predicted values show how scientists do it.

built.title: Today's element and the streak
built.what: One element a day, the same for the whole family, in a three-minute lesson: find it in the table, three questions about it, two elements met before. A streak of days with freezes for a day missed, elements coming back after 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 days, and tomorrow's element as a mystery to guess. The flame in the plaza's dock and the passport; the days follow the account.

built.title: What it cost
built.what: Every built piece now shows what it cost at list price, the model and effort that built it, its size and the dollars for each room or passage, its working time and its agents' tokens, with five stars to rate it; a section compares models and effort levels on the same kind of work. A global ledger and dashboard keep the same record for every project.

built.title: Krypton's hall: seven pictures to step into
built.what: A flask of liquid air boiling away in 1898 until its last drops hide a new gas; the metre measured by krypton's light and then by light itself; why triple windows are filled with it; a satellite pushed along by it; a Saharan water a million years old, dated atom by atom; krypton holding hands with fluorine; and whether kryptonite is real. In the case, a lilac glowing globe and krypton frozen white.

built.title: The diamond press for two
built.what: Carbon's press is a job for two now: one pumps, one works the heater, and the diamond grows only while both are right. Alone you do both; in a room each keeps their job.

built.title: Bible passages in every place
built.what: 46 passages, each about the place it stands in, in the four languages: the NLT for Explorer and the CSB for Scientist in English, and each language's own pair. A verse stone in every hall, one in each wing, the plaza's psalm in the stars behind the table, the lab's and the forges' in their skies, the quiz's and the Atomlings'. Tap one, or press E beside it, for why it is there. Each popup opens its verse in the Bible App, with the whole chapter there.

built.title: The family studio on the game's site
built.what: This studio at element-worlds.vercel.app/studio, for anyone with the link: sign in with your game account (the Pokémon site's works too) to send an idea, a note or a verdict, each kept with who sent it, and Claude answers under it. Each built card now shows the tokens its agents used.

built.title: Iron's hall: seven pictures to step into
built.what: A meteorite of 60 tonnes weighed against elephants and Tutankhamun's dagger from the sky, a ship's deck over the Earth's iron core, an Iron Age smith, iron pulled out of cereal with a magnet, the Eiffel Tower's rivet gang, a rover on red Mars, and a railway welded with thermite. In the case, a meteorite sawn and etched to show its crystals.

built.title: Hydrogen's hall: seven pictures to step into

In the case, a spectrum tube glowing pink-violet.

built.title: The Star Forge
built.what: Make the elements as the universe did: pick a star, tap its core through its burnings, watch it end as a white dwarf or a supernova, catch neutrons slowly in an old giant and all at once when neutron stars collide, and see the table light up by where each element came from.

built.title: Every station worked by hand
built.what: In carbon's and oxygen's wings, the neon workshop and the two video labs you now choose each step by tapping its thing (the pump, a gas flask, the fire triangle's side, the oil tin, the knife), with sliders for what changes smoothly. E still opens the panel with the same steps.

built.title: All seven of oxygen's pictures are doors: every picture on a wall is one now
built.what: Ride a red blood cell from the lung to a muscle; Lavoisier's laboratory and Priestley's burning lens; an Antarctic station where the ozone hole was found and fixed; a sea 2.5 billion years ago rusting into stripes; a bath on a giant balance by a frozen lake; a camp under the northern lights; liquid air, a floating frog and a rocket. Silicon, sodium, carbon and oxygen: 26 rooms.

built.title: All seven of carbon's pictures are doors
built.what: Down to where diamonds are born and up a kimberlite pipe, then a pencil workshop; inside you, inside a leaf, beside a red giant making carbon, an archaeologists' dig dating finds by carbon-14, Smalley's lab where the football molecule was found, and the Mauna Loa observatory with its curve. On an upright phone every station's view now fits its whole width.

built.title: All six of sodium's pictures are doors
built.what: Beside a nerve fibre, Aveiro's salt pans, Davy's lab of 1807, a street under sodium lamps, a mountaintop observatory with its laser star, a baking kitchen.

built.title: All six of silicon's pictures are doors
built.what: The glassblower's workshop, the Earth and Moon from a deck in space, and Silicon Valley by night join the diatoms, the solar hilltop and the silicone kitchen. Every step is chosen by tapping its thing.

built.title: Step into the pictures: the solar hilltop and the silicone kitchen
built.what: Two more of silicon's pictures are doors: a hilltop where you move the sun across the sky, fire light into a giant solar cell and launch Vanguard 1; a kitchen where the silicone tray bends, the silicon snaps and the putty bounces, stretches and sags.

built.title: Step into the pictures: the diatoms
built.what: Silicon's picture "Who lives in a house made of glass?" is a door now: inside, a sunlit sea floor where you open a diatom, make oxygen with sunlight and watch a diatom family shrink and grow big again.

built.title: Doing things together in the worlds
built.what: In a room, the things in every wing are shared: let the balloons go in the neon workshop and everyone there sees them rise; fill a tube, light a word, drop sodium in the bowl, run the chip line, and it happens on everyone's screen. The room keeps its worlds even when nobody is in them, apart from each player's own, which is saved too. Standing beside someone who tries what you have not, a note says it counts once you do it yourself. Videos, panels and the Atomling's words stay each one's own.

built.title: Smooth music on the phone
built.what: The background music crackled on your phone. Each world's music is now made once as a smooth 80 second loop and played with a bigger sound buffer: the phone's sound work is a quarter of what it was, with three times the room before a crackle. The game also counts its own crackles now, so the next session can see whether any are left.

decisions.title: Bigger on the inside
decisions.why: Every cube opens into a hall built from the element's data, so all 118 could be entered from the first day; wings add worlds made for one element.

decisions.title: Characters from real properties
decisions.why: An Atomling's size, colour and hands come from its element's data, so reading a character teaches the element.

decisions.title: Hands are bonds
decisions.why: As many hands as bonds the element usually forms; a molecule is Atomlings holding hands.

decisions.title: Two depths everywhere
decisions.why: Explorer for Artur, Scientist for his father, one switch on every screen.

decisions.title: The science must be right
decisions.why: Numbers from PubChem and mendeleev, facts checked, predictions called predictions.

decisions.title: Things to do, not only to read
decisions.why: Every exhibit is worked by hand: a press, a fire to put out, a breath to hold.

decisions.title: Four languages, always
decisions.why: European Portuguese, English, Polish and German for every word.

decisions.title: The middle stays free
decisions.why: Everything sits at the edges and the world moves into the free part (your notes from the phone).

decisions.title: Pictures over text in the halls
decisions.why: The text boards were boring; picture boards with a hook question instead.

decisions.title: Claude picks, you steer
decisions.why: Claude chooses what comes next and says why; your Sooner, Later and notes change it at any time.

decisions.title: The studio on the game's own site, with the family's accounts
decisions.why: You wanted to share the studio with Artur, who has no Claude account, and to know who made each input. The game already has accounts (the Pokémon site's logins), so the studio is a page of the game: anyone with the link reads it, signed-in accounts send ideas, notes and verdicts kept under their names, and Claude reads and answers them. Your claude.ai studio stays for photos and files.

decisions.title: Which Bibles the other languages quote, and quotations never edited
decisions.why: You chose the NLT for Explorer and the CSB for Scientist. The other languages mirror that pair: an easy, careful translation and a closer one, from each country's own Bible society or publisher (Portugal's, not Brazil's). The words are fetched exactly and never changed.

decisions.title: The whole chapter in the Bible App, not in the game
decisions.why: You asked for the chapter in the popup, then saw it better: open the Bible App right on the verse, where the whole chapter is, with its pictures and more. It also keeps whole chapters out of the game, which the publishers allow only as quotations.

decisions.title: The first station for two: the diamond press
decisions.why: Real diamonds are grown with high pressure and high heat at the same moment, so the press is a job that truly needs two pairs of hands: it teaches the science and makes teamwork the fun. Alone it still works (harder); in a room, each player keeps the job they took, so it needs two.

decisions.title: Today's element: a daily reason to come back, with a streak that forgives
decisions.why: Artur already keeps a Duolingo streak, so the same pull brings him back to the elements: one short lesson a day, the same element for the whole family so it gets talked about, freezes so a missed day does not wipe out weeks, the elements met before coming back on spaced days, and tomorrow's element left as a question to think about in between.
